title: The Lombard League at Legnano
text:
In the mid-twelfth century the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa set out to restore imperial authority over the wealthy, self-governing cities of northern Italy. The cities were bitter rivals, often at war with each other, and some sided with him. In 1162, after a long siege, he took Milan and had much of it destroyed.

His harshness pushed the rivals together. In 1167 a number of cities formed the Lombard League, swearing to defend each other and their liberties. They helped rebuild Milan and founded a new fortified city, named Alessandria after Pope Alexander III, who supported them.

On 29 May 1176, near Legnano, northwest of Milan, Barbarossa's army met the League's forces. The emperor's knights scattered the League's cavalry, then charged the Milanese infantry, who had gathered around the carroccio, a great ox-drawn wagon carrying the city's banner and an altar. The foot soldiers held their ground around it. The League's cavalry, reinforced, returned and struck the imperial army, which broke. Frederick was unhorsed in the fighting and for days was believed dead.

The defeat forced the emperor to negotiate. A truce followed at Venice in 1177, and in the Peace of Constance in 1183 he recognized the cities' right to govern themselves under nominal imperial authority. Before long, though, the cities were again quarreling among themselves.
lesson: Rivals who unite against a common threat can defeat a far stronger power. Holding together after the victory is often the harder test.
people: Frederick Barbarossa, cities of the Lombard League, Pope Alexander III
source: Contemporary chronicles and letters; Gianluca Raccagni, The Lombard League, 1167 to 1225 (2010)
caveat: Popular details such as the 'Company of Death' and its leader Alberto da Giussano come from later legend.
